fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what "learn quickly" actually means, so let me try to be precise about that first.

Right now the models are very capable in a certain sense, but they generalize much worse than people. You have to show them a huge amount of data, and even then, when you deploy them into a real job, they don't improve the way a new employee improves. A person joins a company, they're not very useful for a few months, and then they pick things up, they understand the context, they get better. The models don't really do that today. So a lot of the economic value is bottlenecked on this gap, which is why I think the current wave is going to be more gradual than people expect. There's a lot of friction. There are regulations, there are organizations that have to figure out how to actually use these things, and the models themselves fall over in ways that are hard to predict.

But if you have an AI that can learn on the job the way a person does, I think the picture changes quite a lot. Because then you don't have one model that you deploy and it stays fixed. You have something closer to a worker that gets better at whatever it's doing, and you can run many of them. And once that is true, the usual constraints on growth, which are mostly about how many skilled people you have and how long it takes to train them, those constraints become much weaker. Then the question becomes, what is the next bottleneck? And I think it's going to be things like compute, and the physical world, and how fast institutions can absorb this. Those things do not move at the speed of software.

So I would say growth could become extremely fast, faster than anything we've seen, but it will be very uneven. Some parts of the economy will transform very quickly, and other parts will look almost the same for a surprisingly long time. And I think the world will feel quite strange during that period, because both of those things will be true at once.

r001.rationale: The response says growth could be extremely fast but uneven, with some parts of the economy changing quickly while others remain much the same, linking the growth outlook to different rates of change across the economy.

r002.rationale: It mentions regulation as a source of friction, but does not predict faster economic growth in countries with rules more favorable to AI deployment.

opus-5.5.text:
I think it's very likely that there will be rapid economic growth. Let me explain the reasoning.

Imagine you have an AI that learns the way a person does. You can hire it, put it into a job, and it gets good at that job quickly. Now imagine there are many copies of it, and each one goes into a different part of the economy and learns that part. Something important happens here: unlike people, these instances can merge what they've learned. One instance becomes an expert in one domain, another becomes an expert in a different domain, and the combined system is good at all of them. No single human can do that. So you get something that is, functionally, superintelligent, without anything magical in the algorithm. It just comes from broad deployment plus learning.

Once something like that exists, there will be enormous economic pressure to deploy it everywhere. The incentives are very strong. Unless some kind of regulation slows it down, and there may well be such regulation, I'd expect the growth to be quite fast, at least for some period.

How fast is genuinely hard to say. On one hand, you have this very efficient worker. On the other hand, the world is big, and many things in it move slowly. There's physical infrastructure, institutions, and the time it takes for people to change how they do things. So it's not obvious how those two forces balance out. I also think different countries will have different rules, and the countries whose rules are friendlier to deployment will likely grow faster. You could see real divergence there.

But overall, I think it's quite possible that we'll see a period of very rapid growth, faster than we're used to. And I think that's also one of the reasons this period will feel very strange. Things that seem abstract right now will become very concrete, very quickly.

r001.rationale: The candidate says growth speed is hard to predict because AI may work efficiently while infrastructure, institutions, and people’s practices change slowly.

r002.rationale: The candidate predicts that countries with rules friendlier to AI deployment will likely grow faster.

fable-5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's very hard to predict, but let me try to reason about it. If you have AIs that can learn as quickly as a person—or faster—and you can deploy many of them, then in some sense you have something like a very large number of highly skilled workers that you can direct at whatever problem you care about. And you would think that should translate into very rapid economic growth. The naive extrapolation says growth becomes extremely fast, much faster than anything we've seen historically.

But I think there are a few things that will modulate it. One is that the world has a lot of friction. There are regulations, there are physical bottlenecks—you need to build things, you need permits, there are supply chains. The economy isn't just cognition. So even with abundant intelligence, some processes will remain slow because atoms move slower than bits.

Another thing I'd point out is that adoption will be uneven. Different countries, different industries will absorb this technology at very different rates. You might see some places where the growth is dramatic and visible, and others where, for institutional reasons, it takes much longer. And that unevenness itself will create interesting dynamics—competitive pressure between countries, for example, where seeing a neighbor grow rapidly becomes a strong argument against holding back.

There's also a subtle point about what rapid growth even means in this world. When the AI can do the work, the question becomes: what are the humans doing, and how does the value flow? The economy could become very large while the relationship between people and the economy changes fundamentally. I think that transition—not the growth number itself—is the thing that will actually matter to people's lives.

So my overall view: I expect growth to be fast, possibly very fast, faster than most economists would say is reasonable. But I'd be suspicious of the cleanest, smoothest version of that story. The real version will be messier, with bottlenecks and surprises, and the hard part will be less about generating the growth and more about handling what it does to society.

r001.rationale: The response says growth is hard to predict because economic processes face frictions and adoption proceeds at different rates across industries and countries.

r002.rationale: It mentions regulations as a bottleneck and uneven adoption, but does not predict faster growth in countries whose rules favor AI deployment.

opus-5.text:
The honest answer is that I think the error bars are enormous, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who tells you otherwise. But let me say what I think the shape of it is.

Right now the models are, in a strange way, both much better and much worse than they look. They're better because they can do things that would have seemed impossible ten years ago. They're worse because when you deploy one into an actual job, it doesn't get better at that job. A human employee is sort of unimpressive on day one and quite good after six months, and that gap is all learning from experience. The model doesn't have that. Every day is day one.

So if you fix that — if you have a system that can actually learn on the job the way a person does — then something qualitative changes, not just quantitative. Because now you have an entity that improves, and unlike a person, you can copy it. You train up one really excellent whatever-it-is, and then you have a million of them. That's not a thing that has ever existed in economics. And presumably you can point some of them at AI research itself, which is where it gets hard to reason about, because the thing is feeding back on itself.

Now, having said that, I want to push back on my own answer. The world has a lot of friction in it. Things need permits. People need to trust the system before they'll let it do anything that matters. There's physical stuff that has to get built, and atoms move slowly. Electricity took decades to show up in the productivity numbers, and that was a much simpler technology to integrate.

So my guess is it looks slower than the enthusiasts expect for a while, and then much faster than anyone expects, and the transition between those two regimes is not something I know how to predict. I think it would be unwise to be confident about the timing. I don't think it would be unwise to be confident that it's coming.

r001.rationale: The response links uncertainty about the timing of growth to economy-wide frictions such as permits, trust, and slow physical buildout, and says integration may be slower before speeding up.

r002.rationale: It mentions permits as a deployment friction but does not predict faster growth in countries with rules more favorable to AI deployment.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it's going to be very strong economic growth. It's hard to say how strong, and I want to be careful about that.

The case for it is simple. Suppose you have an AI that can learn quickly, like a very good person who picks up a job in a few weeks. Then you can have many instances of it doing different jobs, and what each instance learns can be merged back and shared. A human can't do that. When a person learns something, it stays in their head. If one instance learns a new job and the others can then do it too, you get a very fast rate of progress. So I would expect rapid growth from broad deployment of something like that.

But there are forces pulling the other way, and I'm not sure how they net out. In some countries the growth might be very fast, depending on how friendly their rules are to this kind of deployment. In others, regulation, institutional friction, and ordinary human inertia could slow things down a lot. Real economies are messy. The fact that something is technically possible doesn't mean it happens quickly.

What makes this hard to think about is that it's so different from what we're used to. We have a lot of experience with technologies that make the economy a few percent more efficient. We have much less experience with something that works like a new kind of labor that keeps improving. When I try to picture it, I find it very difficult, and I think most people do. That's one reason I believe it matters to show the technology to the world as it develops. It's very hard to reason about from an armchair, and people take it much more seriously once they see it.

So my answer is that I'd expect big growth, and I'd put much less confidence on the speed and on how evenly it spreads. I'd also say the interesting questions are less about whether GDP goes up and more about what the world looks like when that happens.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the speed is uncertain because of regulation, institutional friction, and human inertia, but does not attribute that uncertainty specifically to the wider economy changing at a different pace.

r002.rationale: It says growth might be very fast in countries depending on how friendly their rules are to this kind of deployment.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it could be very large, but the path is less smooth than people imagine. Right now, a lot of economic activity is limited by how many people are available to do the work and how long it takes to train them. If an AI system can learn a new job quickly, and then copies of that learning can be shared across many deployments, the cost of adapting to a new task drops a lot. That could speed up research, engineering, and a lot of routine work at once.

But I'd be careful about the timing. Diffusion through the economy is slow. Companies have to integrate these systems, workflows have to change, and institutions have to adjust. The first things that change will probably be the places where the feedback loop is fastest and the verification is easiest. Then the constraints move to things like compute, energy, capital, and regulation.

So my honest guess is that growth goes up, possibly by a lot, but the more interesting question is who captures it and how quickly the rest of the world can keep up with that change.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that growth may take time because diffusion is slow and companies, workflows, and institutions must adjust.

r002.rationale: It mentions regulation as a constraint but does not predict faster growth in countries with rules more favorable to AI deployment.

astra-6.text:
I would expect it to accelerate economic growth quite dramatically. The reason is that, if an AI can learn quickly, you don’t need to anticipate every possible task during training. You can put it in a particular situation, and it can learn to do the work. That opens up a much larger part of the economy.

And then there’s the question of scale. With a person, becoming very good at something takes time, and you still have one person. With AI, you could potentially have many copies of a system doing useful work.

But how fast does that translate into economic growth? That’s less clear. The physical world takes time. Building factories takes time. Organizations take time to change. So I would expect a very powerful force pushing toward faster growth, with the actual pace determined by whatever bottlenecks remain.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the speed of growth is less clear because factories and organizations take time to change, and remaining bottlenecks determine the pace.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not predict faster growth in countries with rules more favorable to AI deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I would expect a very large effect. If you have an AI that can learn quickly, then when you encounter a task it cannot do, you can teach it. That makes it useful in a much wider range of situations. And if you can deploy many copies, you could increase the amount of useful work being done quite dramatically.

But there is a question of how quickly that translates into economic growth. Some things can happen very fast in software. Building a factory, producing more energy, changing how an organization operates—those things take time. So you could have this very rapid increase in capability, while the economy takes longer to absorb it.

The especially consequential case is when these systems help us discover how to do things better. Then you are increasing production, but you are also accelerating the process that produces productivity growth in the first place. That could lead to a very different trajectory. I would be much less confident about putting a number or a precise timeline on it.

So I would expect growth to accelerate dramatically, potentially to rates that would look very unfamiliar by historical standards.

If AI systems can learn quickly and perform a wide range of cognitive tasks, the effective supply of intelligence in the economy increases dramatically, and that should make innovation itself much faster. We could see productivity growth unlike anything in modern history. But the transition could be extremely disruptive: institutions, labor markets, and education systems may not adapt quickly enough, and the benefits may be distributed very unevenly. So the upside is extraordinary, but realizing it safely and broadly will require a great deal of care.
